title: The Index of Coincidence: the geneticist who counted letters, and the cipher cut into his own headstone
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kishinev, a birth under the residence laws
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 September 1891 by Friedman's own signed personnel history, in the NSA declassified documents collection, which gives the birthplace as 'Kishiniev, Russia'. The given name is disputed between sources: Wikipedia has Wolf, the NSA Hall of Honor page has Wolfe. No street or building of birth is documented anywhere located; the coordinate is the city centre.
stops.campa: Wolf Friedman is born on the twenty-fourth of September 1891 in Kishinev, provincial capital of Bessarabia, to Frederick Friedman and Rosa Trust. The empire that registers the birth restricts where Jews may live, what they may study, and which trades they may enter. He leaves as an infant and keeps no memory of the city. The pogrom of 1903 that makes the name Kishinev a byword across the Jewish world happens to a place he cannot picture and never saw with adult eyes. The name entered on the papers is Wolf, or Wolfe; the sources that carry it do not agree.
suggested_refs: Friedman's signed personnel history, NSA declassified Friedman documents, correspondence series
sources: Friedman's signed personnel history via nsa.gov declassified documents
Wikipedia, 'William F. Friedman'

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the family in the new country
stops.date_confidence: the emigration year is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is not resolved here. Wikipedia states the family left Kishinev together in 1892; the dossier's reading of Friedman's personnel history has the father emigrating alone in 1892 and the rest arriving in 1893. The name change is dated 1895 by Wikipedia and tied to the father's 1896 naturalization by the NSA personnel history. Month and day are defaults. Coordinate is downtown Pittsburgh, not a verified address or school building.
stops.campa: The family reaches Pittsburgh and stays. William grows up in the public schools of a steel city, finishes at Pittsburgh Central High, and takes up two things that will matter later without looking as though they will: the sciences, and photography. Somewhere in the middle nineties the name on the family papers changes from Wolf to William, tied by one account to his father's naturalization and by another simply to the third year in the country. Eighteen years of his life pass here and leave almost no documentary trace beyond the schooling.
suggested_refs: Pittsburgh Central High School records for the class of 1910
sources: Wikipedia, 'William F. Friedman'

stops.name: East Lansing, six months at the agricultural college
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1910 entry (Wikipedia). Duration corrected against Irwin Goldman in Genetics (PMC5419462), which gives six months, not the year that circulates in summaries. Month is the ordinary academic start and the day is a default. Coordinate corrected to the historic campus core at Beaumont Tower; the figure carried in the incoming pool sat 3.3 km south of the campus.
stops.campa: He enters Michigan Agricultural College at nineteen, on the agricultural sciences track, and lasts about six months. The college teaches farming as a discipline: soils, breeding, the management of herds and fields. What he wants is the breeding, the part where inheritance can be counted and predicted rather than merely watched. Cornell has a genetics program and Michigan does not, and he transfers before the first academic year is out. What the six months taught him is not recorded anywhere.

stops.name: Ithaca, Cornell and the counting of offspring
stops.date_confidence: attested for the transfer, the 1914 B.S. and graduate work through 1916 (Goldman, Genetics, PMC5419462). Month and day are defaults; the stop covers 1911 to 1916. Coordinate corrected to the Agriculture Quad; the incoming figure lay a kilometre north-east of it toward Fall Creek.
stops.campa: At Cornell's College of Agriculture he studies genetics under the Mendelian and statistical plant-breeding program of the day, takes his B.S. in 1914, and stays on for graduate work and teaching until 1916. The training is arithmetic applied to living material: count the offspring, sort them by trait, compare the observed ratios against what chance alone would produce, and read the difference. He does not know it is a cryptanalytic method. There is no profession of cryptanalysis in the United States in 1916, and no word for it in English either.

stops.name: Cold Spring Harbor, two summers under Davenport
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to detail, attested as to fact: Goldman (Genetics, PMC5419462) places Friedman at the Station for Experimental Evolution in the summers of 1912 and 1913 with Davenport and Shull. Month and day order the stop. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's figure for Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory; the incoming figure landed a kilometre east across the water. No source places Friedman inside the Eugenics Record Office building or in its work; the campus and the funding stream are shared, the department is not.
stops.campa: Two summers at the Carnegie Institution's Station for Experimental Evolution put him under Charles B. Davenport, alongside the maize geneticist George Harrison Shull. The work is frequency work: tabulate what appears, how often, in what company, and let the departure from randomness say what the mechanism must be. Friedman never publishes a word for or against the Eugenics Record Office, which sits on the same funded campus, in a separate department, compiling family pedigrees toward a very different use of the same arithmetic.

stops.name: Geneva, Illinois: Fabyan hires a geneticist
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1915 (Wikipedia, 'William F. Friedman'); the dossier carried the year without the month. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's figure for Fabyan Villa; the incoming figure sat 660 m east, across the Fox River, and is used here for every Riverbank stop in corrected form.
stops.campa: George Fabyan, a textile millionaire with a private estate on the Fox River and money enough to buy himself a scientific establishment, hires the young Cornell geneticist in September to direct plant research and to make photographic records of the work. Riverbank is not a university and answers to nobody. Its departments run to acoustics, levitation, and a standing project to prove that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare and left cipher instructions in the printed type. Friedman is hired for the wheat. The camera is what pulls him across the lawn.

stops.name: Riverbank, Elizebeth Smith and the Gallup readings
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1916 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day are defaults. Bacon's publication of the biliteral cipher in De Augmentis Scientiarum, 1623, is attested independently and is not a claim about Friedman.
stops.campa: Elizebeth Smith, hired to assist Elizabeth Wells Gallup, is at work on Gallup's claim that the mixed typefaces of Elizabethan printing carry Francis Bacon's biliteral cipher, the system in which any two distinguishable things, set in groups of five, can spell any letter of the alphabet. Gallup reads a page one way; another reader reads the same page another way. Elizebeth brings Friedman into the cipher department, and the two of them begin asking the question Gallup does not ask: whether two independent readers, given identical type, arrive at identical plaintext.

stops.name: Riverbank, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1917 (Wikipedia); the exact day and the venue are not established in any source located, and 'probably Illinois' is as far as the pool goes. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: They marry in May 1917, both on Fabyan's payroll, both living on a private estate whose owner regards their working hours as his property and their correspondence as his business. Neither has any formal training in cryptology, because there is nowhere in the country to get any. What they have is her ear for the shapes of Elizabethan printing and his habit of counting things, and between them, over the next four years, the discipline acquires in English most of the working vocabulary it still uses. She keeps her own name in print for the whole of her career. The day of the wedding is not recorded, and neither is the room.
suggested_refs: Elizebeth Smith Friedman's own papers, George C. Marshall Research Library

stops.name: Riverbank, the country sends its ciphers to a private estate
stops.date_confidence: attested that Riverbank served as a de facto federal cryptologic training and research centre after American entry into the war (Wikipedia; NSA monograph DAWNAMERICANCRYPTOLOGY_HATCH.PDF). Month and day order the stop. The index of coincidence is deliberately NOT placed here: it was published in 1922, after Friedman had left the payroll, and the incoming pool's 1917-1918 dating of it is corrected at the 1922 stop. The quote is from lectures given in 1963-65, forty-six years later, and is used for what it says about the period.
stops.campa: The United States enters the war in April with no organized federal codebreaking capability whatever, and for want of anywhere else the War, Navy, and Justice Departments send their intercepts to a private estate in Illinois. Riverbank becomes a training school: Army officers arrive in batches to be taught by two people barely ahead of them. The department solves diplomatic and agent traffic, including messages tied to the German-backed Indian independence network then being prosecuted in the Hindu-German conspiracy trials in San Francisco.
stops.quote: The science of cryptology has not always been regarded as a vital military offensive and defensive weapon, or even as a weapon in the first place.
stops.quote_source: William F. Friedman, 'Six Lectures on Cryptology,' Lecture I, in The Friedman Legacy (NSA, Center for Cryptologic History), delivered 1963-65

stops.name: Aurora, Illinois: the photograph that spells KNOWLEDGE IS POWER
stops.date_confidence: year and place corrected. The incoming geography lens dated this 1917 and placed it at Riverbank in Geneva; William H. The two lenses of the pool contradicted each other and the contradiction is resolved toward the named source, not silently. Month and day are defaults within that winter. Coordinate is central Aurora; no specific field or building is documented.
stops.campa: Seventy-one officers bound for France are lined up in the winter cold with the Friedmans, Fabyan, and two instructors, and told which way to face. Each man is a bit: forward for one value, sideways for the other, five men to a letter, exactly as Bacon set it out in 1623. It is a joke made inside the method under study, by the two people who will shortly demonstrate that the method cannot be read reliably out of a printed page. The line spells KNOWLEDGE IS POWER and runs about four men short of finishing the final R.

segments.name: Chaumont, and the Break with Fabyan

stops.name: Chaumont, the Code and Cipher Solving Section
stops.date_confidence: attested that Friedman was commissioned first lieutenant, National Army, and served in the Code and Cipher Solving Section of G-2 at AEF General Headquarters, Chaumont (Wikipedia; NSA monograph DAWNAMERICANCRYPTOLOGY_HATCH.PDF). The commission is generally placed in May 1918 and the month here orders the stop; the day is a default. The incoming pool carried two separate Chaumont stops a hundred metres apart for the same posting; they are merged here.
stops.campa: Commissioned first lieutenant in the National Army, he crosses to France and reports to the Code and Cipher Solving Section of G-2 at Pershing's General Headquarters at Chaumont. The section works German field codes and ciphers for a staff running an army in contact, which means the product has to be right and it has to be fast, and there is no Fabyan to please. He is twenty-six and has been doing this for two years. A good many of the officers around him learned it from him at Riverbank.

stops.name: Geneva, Illinois: the return and the break
stops.date_confidence: the return date is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is recorded rather than buried. Wikipedia says Friedman returned to the United States in 1920; the NSA monograph places the discharge in April 1919 and the return to Riverbank in May 1919. The 1919 reading is the only one that makes a 1919-1920 Riverbank period possible, and it is the more specific claim, so the stop follows it; the 1920 figure is on the record and is not dismissed.
stops.campa: He comes back to Geneva, Illinois, on promises of back pay and better conditions, and the promises are not kept. Fabyan withholds salary, opens and restricts correspondence, and wants the Baconian findings endorsed rather than tested. The Friedmans stay about eighteen months and then leave, in the winter of 1920 into 1921, with their notebooks and a reputation nobody in Washington has yet learned how to price. The paper he is already drafting will go out two years later under the Riverbank imprint, which is Fabyan's name.

stops.name: Washington, a six-month contract with the Signal Corps
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 (Wikipedia; Friedman's personnel history). The stop is dated to the start of the year as an ordering device; the exact contract date is not in the verified pool. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia's figure for the Main Navy and Munitions Buildings; the incoming figure sat 340 m west of the building's footprint. stops.campa: He signs a six-month civilian contract with the Army Signal Corps in Washington to build the Army's cryptographic systems and write its training material. The Munitions Building on the Mall is a temporary war structure that will stand for fifty years. By 1922 he is the Signal Corps' only cryptanalyst, which is to say that the entire analytic capability of the United States Army is one man at a desk, designing the systems he would himself have to break. The six-month contract is renewed. He stays forty-eight years.
stops.quote: Cryptography is that branch of cryptology that deals with the various means, methods, devices, and machines for converting messages in ordinary, or what we call plain language, into secret language, or what we call cryptograms.

stops.name: Washington, the index of coincidence
stops.date_confidence: corrected dating. The incoming geography lens placed the formulation of the index of coincidence in the 1917-1918 Riverbank stop; it was published in 1922 as Riverbank Publication No. 22, after Friedman had left the payroll, though under the Riverbank imprint. Month and day are defaults. The Vigenere connection is a statement about the class of ciphers the paper breaks, and about the tableau that carries his name, not a claim of any documented engagement between the two men across three and a half centuries.
stops.campa: Riverbank Publication No. 22, The Index of Coincidence and Its Applications in Cryptography, goes out under the imprint of the estate he has already left. It supplies a number: given two stretches of text, how often do letters in the same position match, and does that rate look like a language or like chance. He puts the word cryptanalysis into English in the same years, the solving needing a name distinct from the making. With the index, the polyalphabetic systems descended from Blaise de Vigenere's tableau, held for three centuries to be indecipherable, become a matter of arithmetic.
stops.quote: Cryptology has two main branches: the first is cryptography or, very briefly, the science of preparing secret communications and the second is cryptanalysis or the science of solving secret communications.
stops.quote_source: William F. Friedman, 'Six Lectures on Cryptology,' Lecture I, in The Friedman Legacy (NSA, Center for Cryptologic History), delivered 1963-65

stops.name: Washington, the house on Military Road
stops.date_confidence: the birth dates, Barbara on 14 October 1923 and John Ramsay on 28 July 1926, are carried from the dossier's citation of Friedman's signed personnel statement and were not independently refetched in the research pass; tagged [R] on that ground. The Military Road household by 1927 is attested from Marshall Foundation family photographs. The exact street address was not located and the coordinate approximates the Military Road corridor.
stops.campa: Barbara is born in October 1923 and John Ramsay in July 1926, and by 1927 family photographs place the household on Military Road in northwest Washington, near the park. Both parents go to work on ciphers. The children grow up in a house where what either parent did all day is not discussed at dinner and will not be discussed for decades. Elizebeth's own work moves to the Coast Guard and the Treasury, onto rum-runners and later onto the traffic of German networks in South America, and it is hers, not his.

stops.name: Paris, an errand recorded on a partly illegible form
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Friedman's signed personnel history lists official War Department travel to France, Belgium, and Sweden in 1928, but the scanned form's dates and purposes are partly obscured and no independent account of the itinerary was located. Month, day, and the choice of Paris as the French point are all placeholders, not documented sites. The Hagelin sentence states an independently attested fact about the Swedish firm in the same period and explicitly declines to claim that Friedman saw it.
stops.campa: His signed personnel history records official War Department travel to Europe in 1928, the itinerary listing France, Belgium, and Sweden; the form's dates and purposes are partly obscured on the scan and no fuller account of the trip has surfaced. Sweden in these years is where Arvid Damm's cipher-machine firm is passing into the hands of a young engineer named Boris Hagelin. Whether Friedman saw those machines on that trip cannot be established from the paper that survives. He is watching European cipher machines throughout the decade.

stops.name: Washington, three schoolteachers and a service
stops.date_confidence: corrected and split. The 10 May 1929 date is the War Department directive transferring cryptologic work to the Signal Corps, not the founding of the service with staff; Wikipedia's 'Signal Intelligence Service' article dates the operational start to April 1930, when Friedman began with three junior cryptanalysts. The stop is dated to the directive and states both. Coordinate corrected as at the 1921 stop.
stops.campa: The War Department directive of the tenth of May 1929 moves the government's cryptologic work to the Signal Corps, and in April 1930 the Signal Intelligence Service opens with Friedman as its chief. He teaches the entire subject himself, out of his own textbooks, there being no other place in the country where it is taught. His three junior cryptanalysts are hired off a civil-service examination: Solomon Kullback, Frank Rowlett, Abraham Sinkov. All three are mathematics teachers. None has ever seen a cipher professionally.

stops.name: Washington, the damage assessment on Yardley's book
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and so tagged in herbert_yardley.journey.json, which is where both episodes are staged and where they are also unverified against a primary source. The publication of The American Black Chamber by Bobbs-Merrill in 1931 and the Japanese sales figure are attested; Friedman's damage assessment and his 1941 opposition to Yardley's wartime appointment are not, and are carried here as the other side of a documented professional rivalry. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Herbert Yardley, whose Cipher Bureau the State Department defunded in 1929, publishes The American Black Chamber with Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis and puts the methods, the successes, and the solved Japanese systems into shop windows. It sells thirty-three thousand copies in Japan, where it is read as a confession. Friedman files a grave damage assessment. David Kahn, decades later, finds no worldwide change of codes that followed. Ten years on, when Yardley wants wartime work, Friedman and the British services hold that a man who printed a bureau's secrets belongs nowhere near high-grade material.

stops.name: Washington, punched cards and the machine called RED
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the tabulating machinery: the NSA and Army pages cited for the 1936 introduction of IBM punched-card equipment returned HTTP 403 on every fetch attempted in the research pass, and the claim rests on convergent secondary accounts only. The mid-1930s solution of the Japanese RED diplomatic cipher by SIS is attested in general secondary literature. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The Signal Intelligence Service starts running code and traffic analysis on IBM punched-card tabulating machines, sorting and counting at a rate no room of clerks can match, and the same years see the unit read the Japanese diplomatic machine cipher the analysts call RED. The method is the one he learned counting maize at Cornell: get enough text, count what recurs, and let the departure from chance describe the machine that made it. When exactly the tabulators arrive is not established; the pages that would say so are not open.

stops.name: Washington, the article on Edgar Allan Poe
stops.date_confidence: attested: 'Edgar Allan Poe, Cryptographer', American Literature vol. 8 no. 3, November 1936, listed in the dossier's works list. Day defaults to 01. The stop sits at Friedman's own Washington pin: he audited Poe's ciphers on paper and did not travel to any Poe site, and Fort Moultrie belongs to Poe's own file, not to his.
stops.campa: In the November number of American Literature he publishes 'Edgar Allan Poe, Cryptographer', a working cryptanalyst's audit of the man who in 1839 invited the readers of a Philadelphia weekly to send him ciphers he would undertake to solve, and who built 'The Gold-Bug' around a substitution cipher and a beetle. Friedman goes through the challenges Poe printed and the solutions he claimed and reports what a professional can verify and what he cannot. It is the only literary-historical article of his career.

stops.name: Washington, a cipher with no repetitions in it
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1939 for the changeover and April 1939 for the six most frequent letters (George C. Marshall Foundation, 'Breaking Purple in William Friedman's Own Words', fetched in the research pass). Day defaults to 01. The stop covers both months. The quote is from Friedman's own preliminary historical report of 14 October 1940, reached through that page's excerpt; the original report was not independently located online.
stops.campa: Japan retires the RED machine and puts a new one on the diplomatic circuits. The traffic that comes off it has no usable repetitions at all: none within a message, and where three or four cipher letters do repeat across messages they never stand for the same plaintext. Every technique the unit owns depends on repetition. By April the analysts have got as far as knowing which six letters appear most often, and that is the entire foothold. The Americans call the machine PURPLE, after the color of the binder its traffic goes into.
stops.quote: to the consternation of the cryptanalysts, it was found that not only was there a complete and absolute absence of any causal repetitions within any single message
stops.quote_source: William F. Friedman, 'Preliminary Historical Report on the Solution of the B Machine', 14 October 1940, excerpted by the George C. Marshall Foundation
suggested_refs: Friedman's Preliminary Historical Report on the Solution of the B Machine, 14 October 1940
sources: George C. Marshall Foundation, 'Breaking Purple in William Friedman's Own Words'

stops.name: Washington, the twentieth of September
stops.date_confidence: attested for the discovery of the first repeating sequences on 20 September 1940 from six messages sharing identical indicator text (Marshall Foundation). Genevieve Grotjan's discovery is real, well attested elsewhere, and conventionally dated to the same day, but the Marshall Foundation page does not name her at all: it deliberately credits the group. Her attribution here is therefore carried on the general literature, not on the source cited beside it, and the incoming pool's citation of the Marshall page for her was a misattribution and is corrected.
stops.campa: After eighteen months, six messages sharing identical indicator text are laid side by side, and the first repeating sequences in PURPLE come out of them. On the same day Genevieve Grotjan, working through the worksheets, finds the structural pattern the reconstruction has been missing. What the section is building is not a captured machine but an inference: a device nobody in the room has ever seen, described entirely from the shape of what it emits. Rowlett has run the daily work. Friedman has directed it and, for months, has not been sleeping.
stops.quote: a statistical calculation gave the astonishing result that the number of repetitions actually present in these cryptograms was less than the number to be expected had the letters comprising them been drawn at random out of a hat!
stops.quote_source: William F. Friedman, 'Preliminary Historical Report on the Solution of the B Machine', 14 October 1940, excerpted by the George C. Marshall Foundation
suggested_refs: The PURPLE worksheets, National Cryptologic Museum

stops.name: Washington, two translations and a machine built from switches
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27 September 1940 (Marshall Foundation, fetched in the research pass, which confirms the date and Friedman's own refusal of individual credit). The completion of a working analog in 1940 is attested by the same source without a month; the attribution to Leo Rosen and the section's engineers is from the general literature and the dossier, not from the fetched page.
stops.campa: Two complete translations of B-machine traffic are finished on the twenty-seventh of September, and the Japanese diplomatic cipher is solved. Leo Rosen and the section's engineers have already built an analog out of telephone stepping switches, a machine that reads incoming PURPLE as fast as it arrives, assembled from parts bought over a counter. Friedman writes the preliminary historical report on the fourteenth of October, and in it he declines to name any single person as deserving the major portion of the credit.
stops.quote: the successful solution... is the culmination of 18 months of intensive study by a group of cryptanalysts and assistants working as a harmonious, well-coordinated and cooperative team. Only by such cooperation and close collaboration of all concerned could the solution possibly have been reached, and the name of no one person can be selected as deserving of the major portion of credit for this achievement.

stops.name: Walter Reed, the neuropsychiatric section
stops.date_confidence: the month is attested: Wikipedia's 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman' article gives January 1941 and two and a half months in the ward. The exact admission date of 4 January that the incoming pool carried is not supported by anything fetched and is downgraded to the month; the day is a default. The retrospective label of bipolar disorder found in some later writing is not a contemporary diagnosis and is not asserted.
stops.campa: In January he is admitted to the neuropsychiatric section at Walter Reed General Hospital and stays about two and a half months. The record calls it a nervous breakdown; the accounts around it say exhaustion, and a depression running back into the thirties. He is forty-nine. He is discharged into a war that is eleven months from Pearl Harbor and returns to work with the operational direction of the section in other hands. No clinical record of the admission is public, and none of the accounts was written by him.

stops.campa: The Army takes over a girls' junior college on Glebe Road on the tenth of June 1942, and Arlington Hall becomes the headquarters of American cryptanalysis. The service Friedman started with three schoolteachers grows into thousands: mathematicians, linguists, chess players, crossword compilers, and above all women recruited out of colleges and typing pools, who do the bulk of the work at the machines. He is consulted constantly and commands nothing. His posts here are senior research posts.
